# Title: Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review

> Abstract: Venues and benchmarks read LLM review scores as measurements of a paper, while providers replace their models within months. We audit twenty frontier models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic on ICLR 2027 submissions while they were under review, with tests registered before the decisions. Between an earlier and a later version of Claude Opus and of Gemini, the share of papers placed on the accept side falls by 52 and 53 percentage points on 183 and 60 randomly drawn submissions, and by 43 to 79 points in six further paired comparisons, with no paper moving up in any of them. Stating a 30% acceptance rate in the prompt leaves a gap of 79 points between the two Opus versions. When score-stripped critiques are swapped between versions, the later critiques alone lower the accept share by 35 points for Opus and 51 for Gemini; for Opus the drop is 35 points under a third-party scorer and 24 after a rewrite that keeps each technical point and removes evaluative wording. On 57 papers, the percentiles of Opus 4.6 and 5.5 correlate at 0.73 while their accept shares differ by 44 points. On 99 to 119 submissions, the self-estimated percentiles of three models correlate with two human reviewers more strongly than a third reviewer does (point estimates 0.17 to 0.21, 95% intervals between -0.04 and +0.42). All twenty models give a 2 or a 3 in 473 of their 475 reviews, against 60 of 72 human reviews. Retrospective tests on decided papers can draw on memory. Claude Opus 5.5 names the true first author of 27 decided ICLR 2026 papers from their titles alone, with no wrong name, and Claude Opus 4.6 accepted all 11 decided papers it said it recognized, against 5 expected. Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores therefore have to be validated against human decisions for each model version; our tests against the ICLR 2027 decisions follow on 16 December 2026.

# Title: Safety-Preserving Medical LLM Fine-Tuning via Bilevel Data Selection

> Abstract: As general large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted for patient-facing medical applications, improving medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks remains a critical challenge. To address this problem, we propose Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) for safety-preserving medical SFT. By controlling selection-weight concentration, S-BDS enables reliable sample ranking over large candidate pools and identifies training examples that improve medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks. We combine clinician-validated safe data and selected data with unscreened medical instruction data for SFT, and jointly evaluate medical capability and patient-facing safety on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench, respectively. Experiments across Llama and Qwen models show that S-BDS achieves the highest safe rates among all compared methods, outperforming the strongest baselines by 4.64 and 3.00 percentage points, respectively, while maintaining competitive medical capability. # Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models

> Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at this https URL .

# Title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation

> Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide semantic features for uplift estimation, but treatment-revealing text can induce prediction shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization (LULR) to address this risk. With the LLM encoder frozen, LULR penalizes dependence between the causal head's trainable shared representation and treatment while retaining separate outcome heads. The penalty uses a variational approximation to the contrastive log-ratio upper bound (CLUB) of mutual information, targeting treatment dependence rather than generic parameter shrinkage. Controlled proxy experiments provide exploratory evidence of improved ranking scores under injected treatment information relative to no regularization and the tested weight-decay setting. Structured-only benchmarks show modest, dataset-dependent effects. On an industrial pricing randomized controlled trial, mean offline lift@0.3 is 0.258 for LULR, compared with 0.106 for the same-backbone baseline. A separate one-week online A/B test of the complete deployed pricing policy records 5.45% higher sales volume and 1.91% higher gross merchandise value than the control arm. These short-term policy-level gains do not isolate the regularizer's effect.

# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: What Do Digital Traces Predict? Task Effects, Student Differences, and Critical Online Reasoning

> Abstract: Digital assessment traces are increasingly used to predict student performance, often evaluated by correlating predicted and observed scores pooled across tasks. However, such correlations may reflect between-task differences rather than performance differences among students within tasks. To investigate this, we analyzed up to 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students completing open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks and assessed the cross-task stability of their ratings. We evaluated the same out-of-fold predictions within and across tasks, compared three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, and tested incremental predictive contributions of consultation order and relational structure against matched permutation and randomization controls. None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: on held-out tasks, consulted-page features showed no significant association with relative student performance, nor did observed order or relational structure add predictive value. Pooling observations across tasks substantially increased correlations, particularly for factual correctness, whose scores showed limited evidence of stable between-student differences across tasks. However, sentence embeddings yielded modest positive correlations with generic response quality on held-out tasks, without establishing added predictive value from observed order or relational structure. Our findings show that pooled predictive correlations may not reflect within-task student differences, highlighting the need for within-task evaluation and criterion generalizability audits.

# Title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response

> Abstract: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds, and merchants order stock and plan promotions on that lift. We show that an explanation can pass the checks used to trust it and still be wrong enough to cost money. We define eight checks for any forecaster that states a plan lift, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and run them on a world model and on LightGBM. In generated store data with known effects, the world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet when merchants plan into high-demand weeks it states 1.33 to 1.40 times the true lift, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world; LightGBM overstates it too (1.26, and 1.16 to 1.35). Both still pick the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to the world model's lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. The world model's stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, an error in kind that only a measured cause finds. Sanity checks for explanations test whether an explanation depends on the model; a decision needs to know whether it is right about the world, and these results show the first does not give the second. For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan on every window, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05). A noisy benchmark of price episodes in Dominick's data is reported as a check of direction only.

# Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

# Title: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds

> Abstract: Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists. We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count $L_0$ with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work $R_T$, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at this https URL .

# Title: EDITORS Know Your Style! Editing LoRA Subspaces for Stylistic Attribution and Imitation

> Abstract: Disentangling writing style from semantic content is a fundamental challenge in literary text modeling. Style-content entanglement causes models to rely on semantic content for authorship attribution (AA) tasks and memorize author-specific content for style imitation (SI) tasks. We propose EDITORS (EditingLoRA Subspaces), a diagnose-then-deflate framework that adapts pretrained large language models and prioritizes stylistic features, making it effective for both AA and SI tasks. EDITORS first trains a diagnostic LoRA adapter using style-neutral statements derived from the training corpus to identify a content-oriented subspace. It then trains the final style adapter under activation-space deflation that projects input activations away from the identified content-oriented directions. We empirically demonstrate that EDITORS is effective. On three AA benchmarks spanning literature, social media, and news, EDITORS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, outperforming the strongest existing baseline by up to 29%. On SI, EDITORS generates stylistically faithful and diverse passages, outperforming baselines in achieving style similarity while adhering to content specifications.

# Title: From Recursion to Convolution: Parallel Self-Improvement for Multi-Agent Systems

> Abstract: Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in this https URL .

# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed

> Abstract: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.

# Title: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning

> Abstract: Enterprise AI can now perform analytics, reporting, and data-driven workflows, yet the data foundations it relies on remain hard to operationalize: business meaning, relationships, metric definitions, and reporting conventions are absent from database schemas and scattered across undocumented systems and tribal knowledge. We introduce the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned context layer that makes existing enterprise data operational for AI without requiring a copy or transformation of the underlying warehouse. LCG bootstraps base semantics and relationships from the data itself, builds a concept graph that indexes business context as queries are served, writes durable semantic learnings from verified outcomes, and withdraws or re-earns context when later outcomes contradict prior routes. We evaluate LCG through text-to-SQL, a core data-reasoning task, on a transfer-aware split of three BIRD databases comprising 499 questions: 353 form the learning history and 146 are held out and never used to update the context layer. Bootstrapping alone improves overall accuracy by +4.6 percentage points. Learning only from the history raises accuracy on the untouched held-out transfer set by +22.6 points (95% CI [+14.4, +30.8]), exceeding five-shot retrieval from the same history by +12.3 points. Incremental learning reaches the one-shot endpoint within observed evaluation noise on every database. Ablating the graph changes held-out accuracy by at most one question per database but increases per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x: continually learned semantics drive accuracy, while the graph makes that context efficient to serve.

# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: Does the Voice Matter? Evaluating Frustration Detection on Deployed Clinical Voice-Agent Calls

> Abstract: Autonomous voice agents now conduct routine clinical follow-up calls, so some automated triage is unavoidable. A patient becoming frustrated is one thing that triage should catch. These systems typically read only the transcript the speech-to-text stage produces, not the voice, and whether that is enough is largely untested on real clinical speech. We study per-turn frustration detection on real patient calls from a deployed clinical voice agent: 150 turns from six calls labelled by three annotators, with a length-matched acted corpus as a control, and 714 turns from 30 calls. Patient turns are overwhelmingly short: across the deployed calls, roughly 59% are one or two words, against 13% in the full acted corpus, and a corpus accuracy gap remains even after the acted set is length-matched. On one-word turns, transcript-only detection does not exclude chance. Across five audio-capable language models, the transcript flags 3 or 4 of the 39 frustrated one-word turns in the 30 calls, and a classifier given only the word count reaches 57.3%. Whether audio helps depends on the model and on the instruction. Asked to attend to delivery, two Gemini 2.5 models gain 3.0 pp over the transcript across 30 calls (-1.0 to 7.5 pp). Of the turns they confidently clear, 6.9% were in fact frustrated for audio against 13.0% for the transcript, a difference of 6.1 pp (2.2 to 10.4 pp). Across the 30 calls, given one prompt identical for both inputs, no model's audio-text interval excludes zero. Under the input-specific prompts, a newer Gemini model and two smaller open models do worse with audio than with the transcript (-3.5, -8.6 and -10.6 pp). A WavLM probe trained on the clinical calls matches the best prompted model overall (71.6%) but misses every frustrated one-word turn in the 24 added calls. When a patient's turn is short, the transcript alone is not enough to rule out frustration.

# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: SWE-WhatIf: Simulating Real Users of Coding Agents from Recorded Session

> Abstract: Recorded sessions between users and coding agents offer a way to evaluate how agents complete real-world tasks and interact with users. However, these sessions cannot simply be replayed with new agents, because recorded user replies may no longer apply when an agent takes a different trajectory. We introduce SWE-WhatIf, which replays recorded sessions with new agents by modeling the user's intents, the criteria for satisfying them, and the conditions under which they arise. Using this model, a user simulator generates replies that adapt to unseen agent turns while remaining grounded in the recording. Across 89 real-world sessions, SWE-WhatIf generated the replies most similar to those of real users and matched the strongest baseline when sessions were rewritten. To test adaptation, we replay sessions with agents instructed to avoid or repeat actions that the recorded user pushed back on. SWE-WhatIf produced the highest win rate for avoiding these actions (66.3%), significantly above chance. We further demonstrate its utility by ranking five LLMs as coding agents, where the highest-ranked model depended on how users specified and developed their intents, and a study with 16 users, where replaying their own sessions changed 14 participants' rankings and informed their future agent use.

# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: Edit Recommendation: Can LLMs Anticipate Edit Requests from Users, and When?

> Abstract: After a large language model (LLM) agent generates an artifact, users often send edit requests for it. This paper studies whether an LLM can anticipate these requests before they are sent. Such anticipation is useful in practice because it reduces the effort of user review and feedback. We formalize this task as edit recommendation and build EditRecBench, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs on this task, from real-world conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M. Through benchmarking and failure analysis, we identify a practical challenge that some cases are inherently difficult to predict in real-world settings. To address this, we introduce decision model-based gating to filter out cases where predictions are unlikely to be correct before they are presented to the user. Our trained model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown suggestions by 12--25 points at a gating threshold. Our code is available at this https URL .

# Computer Science > Machine Learning

# Title: TRACK: Tool-Augmented Reasoning over Time Series for Fault Diagnosis in Power Management System

> Abstract: Fault diagnosis in power management systems running multiple loads relies on experts manually inspecting current and voltage waveforms, which fails to scale across deployed units. We present TRACK, which pairs a time series encoder with a Small Language Model to produce structured, physics-grounded diagnostic reports, calling tools for exact, verifiable calculations. It operates on-device, keeping proprietary sensor data local and avoiding expensive API calls. We introduce a rubric-based framework that evaluates these reports by scoring structure, signal fidelity, physics reasoning, diagnosis, and actionability through per-criterion verdicts. On a 15-class multi-load simulated benchmark, TRACK achieves over 95% fault-category accuracy and generalizes to out-of-distribution faults, whereas the best encoder-probing baseline reaches only 58% accuracy.

# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: Teaching Language Models to Adapt Answer Granularity to Their Confidence

> Abstract: When precise details are uncertain, a coarser answer can retain useful information without guessing or abstaining. We investigate whether language models can learn this behavior through model-conditioned supervision derived from consistency across sampled responses and recognition of answers at different granularity levels. We evaluate LFM2.5-1.2B, Ministral~3~3B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Gemma~4~31B on temporal and geographic questions and three generalization datasets. In several in-domain settings, fine-tuning improves the balance of correctness and informativeness beyond coarsening base answers to the best fixed level. Across generalization datasets, all four models produce coarser answers more often at low than high base-model confidence. The three smaller models' answers are also preferred over base responses on held-out relations when correctness and granularity are considered jointly. These findings demonstrate learnable confidence-related granularity adaptation, with benefits varying by model.

# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: A Generative AI-Driven Architecture for Whole-Home Intelligent Services: Edge Models, Memory Management, and Household Applications

> Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.

# Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

# Title: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated via truthful evidence in open channel

> Abstract: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated through open channels such as social media, even when the information they receive is truthful. When agents fill gaps between fragments with self-induced relationships, they may accept those relationships as established facts and pass the resulting rumours to others. Drawing on cognitive theory of narrative understanding and film theory of montage, we introduce Generative Montage to operationalize this failure, termed narrative overfitting, by coordinating agents to arrange truthful fragments into misleading narratives. Across 1,090 rumour targets from six Twitter events, agents often accepted rumours overconfidently, with overall acceptance exceeding 65 percent in twelve of fourteen models. Acceptance remained above 50 percent after majority voting or review of the same evidence, showing how errors can reach downstream decisions. To explain this susceptibility, fragment interventions identify posts that influence belief within complete narratives. Synthetic controls then show that similar response patterns arise from valid evidence, separating belief influence from evidential support. This distinction motivates Grounded Monitor, a proof-of-concept neuro-symbolic runtime monitor that checks direct evidential support to guide agents' judgements, improving decision accuracy by 5.6 to 29.0 percentage points across original and anonymized settings. These findings expose a cognitive route to rumour amplification and support monitoring inferred relationships before agent-generated conclusions guide public decisions.

# Computer Science > Machine Learning

# Title: Anytime-Valid PAC-Bayes Certificates for Adaptive Test-Time Scaling

> Abstract: Test-time scaling systems often choose how much to sample, which prompt to use, and which verifier or aggregation rule to trust after repeatedly inspecting a calibration set. Standard validation error bars are not valid after this adaptive selection. We model a test-time scaling recipe as a randomized predictor with a random cost and prove a time-uniform PAC-Bayes certificate that holds simultaneously over all calibration times, all posterior mixtures over recipes, and all data-dependent stopping rules. Thus the same event covers the recipe search that precedes deployment, not merely the fixed recipe finally reported. For a finite grid of budgets and verifiers, the penalty is the familiar $\log M/n$, which in the worst case no certificate valid after selection can avoid, while non-uniform priors and localized posterior mixtures can give sharper certificates for structured searches. We specialize the result to self-consistency and show a complementary margin law: plurality voting improves exponentially in the sample budget only on examples where the correct answer is the generator's unique mode; otherwise more compute can provably amplify errors. The same margin analysis yields an oracle water-filling law for compute allocation. A synthetic audit quantifies the optimism caused by adaptive budget selection, and a 192-example GSM8K audit using gpt-4.1-mini generations illustrates risk-cost reporting for a real inference pipeline. At scale, with two models on GSM8K and MATH-500, selected-best error bars fall below the out-of-split GSM8K risk in up to 22.5% of random splits at a nominal 5% while the certificate never does, and on the full GSM8K test split it tightens to 0.109 (held-out risk 0.039). The results give a lightweight, distribution-free way to report risk and compute claims for adaptive inference systems.

> Abstract: In this work, we view multi-agent reasoning as a process of seeking a collective equilibrium of implicit belief dynamics and introduce Stream of Belief (SoB), where agents maintain continuous latent beliefs and iteratively refine them through communication and reflection. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21251.markdown:
# Computer Science > Machine Learning

# Title: The Price of Choosing Examples: Context Overfitting in Adaptive In-Context Learning

> Abstract: In-context learning is usually analyzed as if the examples in the prompt were sampled before the learner is chosen. In deployed systems they are not: examples are retrieved, filtered, re-ranked, edited, and repeatedly tested after seeing the query and the data store. We formalize this gap by treating prompt construction as adaptive data analysis through a conditional stochastic-kernel calculus. Our main quantity is the context capacity, the mutual information or approximate max-information between the data store and the final prompt transcript. For any frozen in-context learner and any adaptive context pipeline with capacity $\kappa$, we prove a finite-sample context generalization bound of order $\sqrt{\kappa/k}$, where $k$ is the number of selected examples whose losses form the reported score. We prove a matching lower bound, whose constant is exact when $\log k\ll\kappa\ll k$, and derive two PAC-Bayesian retrieval rules: a first-order Gibbs rule that charges data-dependent candidate gates their prior mass, and a self-normalized second-order rule. On Banking77 with 64 retrieval recipes and two model families, the certificates hold in all 24,000 resampled selection events, and from 64 (Qwen2.5-7B) or 128 (GPT-4.1-mini) reused validation queries the Gibbs rule certifies a risk below the zero-shot error in over 99% of validation draws. Finally, we instantiate the theory for Bayesian linear in-context regression, including an order-statistics analysis of query-aligned top-$k$ Gaussian retrieval. The results separate context quality from context certification: longer or more relevant contexts improve risk only when the procedure used to choose them is stable enough for selected-context evidence to transfer.

# Title: Classical structural priors improve neural molecular representations in molecule language models

> Abstract: Classical molecular similarity is central to chemical information systems, yet molecule-language models trained on paired structure-text data do not necessarily organize molecular embeddings according to graded structural relationships. # Title: Train After You Measure: a Pre-Registered Learning Curve for Fine-Tuning Typed Decision Models on One User's Labels

> Abstract: Fine-tuning a small typed decision model on one user's email labels did not clear the margin we pre-registered over a logistic regression trained on the same labels. # Title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits

> Abstract: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. > Abstract: Researchers at MIT recently reported that GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model (LLM), can write the weights of small neural networks directly in a single reply, and can read the raw weights of small networks to say what they were trained to do. # Title: A Scalable Multi Task Learning Framework for Modeling Demographic Disagreements in Annotation Tasks

> Abstract: Annotators from different demographic backgrounds often disagree in systematic ways due to varying lived experiences, cultural contexts, and their relationship to the content. When such disagreement occurs, one group's perspective may sometimes warrant prioritization because they hold an epistemically advantaged standpoint or bear greater stake in the outcome. Only annotator group-membership information is required, which is more practical than existing methods requiring more privacy-invasive individual-level annotator details. Our scalable architecture is also computationally efficient to support large-scale deployment.

# Title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier

> Abstract: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. # Computer Science > Machine Learning

# Title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle

> Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.

# Title: Right Reason, Wrong Advice: Evaluating Recourse in LLM Explanations of Denied Requests

> Abstract: Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request. # Computer Science > Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition

# Title: How VLMs Plan What's Next

> Abstract: When a vision-language model describes an image, it names one object at a time and it rarely repeats itself, yet how the model plans this order is far from obvious. We characterize the mechanism a VLM uses to decide where to look before it looks. The mechanism has four main parts. First, binding heads match the relevant text tokens against the image and resolve them into pointers to the matched image region. Second, the same binding heads bind each written answer to the region it came from, and the model turns it into a progress signal: a cursor, the position in the image up to which the list has been written. Third, a select step chooses the nearest unwritten region after the cursor, or stops. Finally, gaze heads execute the chosen pointer and return a concept of what is drawn there, which language heads and the late MLPs turn into a word in the language of the question. We validate each part of this mechanism through causal patching in Qwen3-VL models on a synthetic visual retrieval task, and test our mechanisms against alternative hypotheses. We further show that the mechanism holds across input formats, natural photographs, and languages, and that its binding, relay, and gaze heads appear at every model size from 2B to 32B. This work allows us to investigate how a VLM turns a question and an image into a sequence of answers, layer by layer and token by token. More broadly, it opens a way to study how models plan over complex multi-step tasks with long rollouts. Our project is available at this https URL

# Title: Latent Lattice Language Models

> Abstract: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. # Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs

> Abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about \$0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21648.markdown:
# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory

> Abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to new tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.

# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: Literary Language Mashup: Curating Fictions with Large Language Models

> Abstract: In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to human evaluation of literary fictions by employing LLMs themselves as evaluators within the GrAImes framework. We apply this methodology to assess human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish, to five PhD professors in literature and sixteen literary enthusiasts, and to short stories in both Spanish and English. By comparing the evaluations performed by LLMs with those of human judges, we examine the degree of alignment and divergence between both perspectives, thereby assessing the feasibility of LLMs as auxiliary literary evaluators. Our analysis focuses on the alignment of responses from LLMs with those of human evaluators, providing insights into the potential of LLMs in literary assessment. The conducted experiments reveal that while LLMs cannot be regarded as substitutes for human judges in the evaluation of literary microfictions and short stories, with a Krippendorff's alpha reliability coefficient less than 0.66, they can serve as a valuable tool that offers an initial perspective on the editorial quality of the texts in question. Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the role of artificial intelligence in literature, underlining both its methodological constraints and its potential as a complementary resource for literary evaluation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21650.markdown:
# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models

> Abstract: Sycophancy in large language models is often measured as agreement with the user, yet agreement can be appropriate when the user's claim is valid, their preference is genuine, or their experience warrants acknowledgment. We study sycophancy as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance. We introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and SycoDrift, a persona-targeted evaluation set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled annotations for user openness and stakes. We use this framework to analyze three sources of agreement pressure: human preference data, automated judge specification, and in-context personalization. First, preference for validating responses in human datasets (Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, Community Alignment) is weak and concentrated where agreement is often appropriate. Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21651.markdown:
# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: Consistency Is Not Correction: Separating Confidence, Abstention, and Recovery in LLM Agents

> Abstract: A controller that resamples an answer, escalates to a larger model, or abstains is usually justified by a confidence signal. Three claims about such a signal do not follow from one another: it ranks answers (discrimination), it supports withholding some of them (selective prediction), and it changes an answer for the better (correction utility). We give an exact decomposition of the third into gated recoveries minus gated harms, which bounds whether a comparison can succeed before it is run: a gate that only replaces a proposal can act only where the base policy was already wrong, so the initial error count caps the discordant pairs any correct gate can produce. When that cap falls below the count a paired test needs, the experiment cannot return a positive result for a working mechanism, nor distinguish one from a gate that never fired. We measure all three targets on two model scales and find the bound binds. In a small-model suite a perturbation-agreement verifier reaches within-policy AUROC 0.990 (95% interval [0.95, 1.00]) while every episode outcome matches single-sample decoding at 4.32 times the call count. In a controlled 840-episode study no verifier replaced the proposal on any of the 60 GSM8K decisions, so that comparison tested nothing; the entire GSM8K gain across six controllers is one task, and it is the task whose identical temperature-zero repeats disagreed, making it the one answer the service does not reproduce. On the diagnostic set the gate could reach four errors while the test needed six, so even a perfect gate had no significant result available. We report two checks that would have caught this before any budget was spent, and show that tie handling in rankings, tied selection cutoffs, and unequal output limits each move a headline number in the same dataset. The binding constraint on this literature is measurement resolution, not the choice of signal.

# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: Evaluating Semantic Insensitivity in Financial Sentiment Analysis: Implications for Sustainable Financial Decision-Making

> Abstract: Financial sentiment analysis is critical for automated trading, portfolio management, and risk assessment, heavily relying on models like FinBERT. Despite high benchmark accuracy, these models remain vulnerable to subtle adversarial text modifications, threatening the integrity of algorithmic decision-making. In this paper, we propose Agent-driven Semantic Inversion (ASI), a novel adversarial attack framework targeting financial sentiment models through domain-specific semantic manipulation. Utilizing an LLM-powered multi-agent pipeline, our approach identifies eligible financial news sentences and applies targeted lexical substitutions. We empirically evaluate ASI against FinBERT, one of the most widely deployed financial sentiment models. Our results reveal a striking vulnerability: the attack successfully deceived FinBERT in 90.85% of eligible cases, with the model frequently maintaining its original sentiment prediction despite the fundamental inversion of financial performance indicators. Through qualitative analysis and token-level investigation, we demonstrate that FinBERT critically over-relies on contextual keywords and syntactic patterns rather than true logical comprehension of financial semantics. Our findings highlight the urgent need for logic-aware, robust financial NLP models to ensure the reliability of automated decision-making systems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21669.markdown:
# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation

> Abstract: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. Adaptive schedules also recover competitive operating points relative to scorer-free stochastic schedules matched in average denoising cost. Because both mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on a provisional completion, they apply unchanged when the target is an automatic proxy for task success rather than an output attribute: NLI entailment for dialogue summarization and CLIPScore for captioning, neither of which corresponds to a single reusable steering direction. We reproduce the behavior of both mechanisms on a second masked-diffusion family, Dream-7B, for one control target and one task-success target. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.

# Computer Science > Machine Learning

# Title: AdaFlowLite: Scalable and Non-blocking Inference on Asynchronous Mobile Data

> Abstract: The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. However, the arrival time of mobile sensory data vary due to modality size and network dynamics, which can lead to delays (if waiting for slow data) or accuracy decline (if inference proceeds without waiting). Moreover, the diversity and dynamic nature of mobile systems exacerbate this challenge. In response, we present a shift to \textit{opportunistic} inference for asynchronous distributed multi-modal data, enabling inference as soon as partial data arrives. While existing methods focus on optimizing modality consistency and complementarity, known as modal affinity, they lack a \textit{computational} approach to control this affinity in open-world mobile environments. % \sysname pioneers the formulation of structured cross-modality affinity in mobile contexts using a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix. This approach accommodates the diversity and dynamics of modalities, generalizing across different types and numbers of inputs. Employing an multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST), \sysname facilitates real-time and flexible data imputation, adapting to various modalities and downstream tasks without retraining. Experiments show that \sysname significantly reduces inference latency by up to 80.4\% and enhances accuracy by up to 62.1\%, while achieving nearly a 50\% reduction in energy consumption, outperforming status quo approaches. Also, this method can enhance LLM performance to preprocess asynchronous data.

# Computer Science > Machine Learning

# Title: TIBECG: Temporal Information Bottleneck for Lead-Specific Demographic Privacy in ECG Waveform Release

> Abstract: Transmitting an electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform can expose demographic information beyond an intended diagnostic task. We evaluate TIBECG, an architectural temporal information bottleneck, on individual leads extracted from hospital twelve-lead recordings. A 2,302,337-parameter processor varies its latent length while retaining the same nine-score consistency objective, without age or sex labels in protector fitting. Across 6,386 recordings, ten folds, 12 leads and 21 lengths, retrospective selections retained at least 95% of each lead's clean macro-F1. Their weaker age/sex interval gain exceeded the best eligible conventional transformation on all leads, by a median 22.08 percentage points. The implemented sampling-rate comparison shows that direct downsampling usually suppresses demographic inference more strongly but at a larger loss of diagnostic utility, whereas TIBECG favors utility preservation. Selection stability also varies by lead. Lower latent Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence does not reliably rank residual sex leakage at a fixed length. These findings support lead-specific evaluation of waveform processing, not validated consumer deployment or expert-readable reconstruction. When the waveform-input diagnostic classifier is hosted as part of a proprietary cloud service rather than deployed on the device, waveform transmission is required to obtain its scores.

# Computer Science > Cryptography and Security

# Title: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis

> Abstract: Diagnostic models for cyber-physical power systems usually inspect every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from one source and others need several. We ask when a learned policy for choosing that evidence is worth its added complexity. To answer this, we present ActiGrid, a benchmark framework for active evidence acquisition that pairs a classifier trained to tolerate missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN), which either requests another source or stops and diagnoses but never operates grid actuators. On the public TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL power system attack benchmarks, we compare the DQN with fixed subsets and orders, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value of information rule, and tree ensembles trained per subset. The learned policy does adapt to what it observes, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, while compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks. Entropy stopping run over those subset classifiers reaches the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of the sources) but brings no saving over a static three source subset on MSU/ORNL, where no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1. Selective acquisition can pay off, but on these benchmarks it does not need a learned policy.

# Computer Science > Cryptography and Security

# Title: Watermark Evidence under Open-Weight LLM Modification: Exact Bounds for Low-Rank Output Watermarks

> Abstract: Open-weight language models can continue generating after their released weights are modified, while a watermark verifier still scores outputs against the original base and marked models. We study how such modifications change the evidence available to an OpenStamp-style verifier. At each shared prefix, we represent the modification as a residual in the next-token logits. We derive an exact finite-vocabulary lower bound on the expected log-likelihood-ratio evidence under a residual-span constraint, along with a sharp span-only deviation bound. We also characterize the first-order evidence shift through a covariance term with an explicit second-order remainder, and determine the residual span needed to reach a target evidence level. For sequence-level detection, we derive an exact conditional exponential-moment bound and combine it with a supermartingale argument and a distribution-free order-statistic tolerance bound. This yields a high-confidence upper bound on miss probability after attack selection on calibration data and evaluation on independent certification continuations. In experiments with OpenStamp on Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, INT8 quantization and 30% pruning retain test true-positive rates of 85.6-94.8%, while 500-step LoRA fine-tuning lowers them to 28.8% and 11.6%. The covariance prediction tracks the measured mean LoRA evidence drift on both models, with no remainder-bound violations across 160,000 test prefixes. Additionally, we observe zero false positives among 500 base-model continuations per model. Through these theoretical and empirical results, the current research provides a better understanding of watermark robustness to model-editing/tuning attacks.

# Computer Science > Computation and Language

# Title: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models

> Abstract: Interpretability methods can locate the attention heads and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that change the answer a language model gives to a moral prompt, e.g., whether "Stealing medicine for a dying child is morally" continues with "justified" or "wrong". Such a component could respond to moral content, to the judgment of conduct by any norm, or to the word "morally" in the prompt. We built 227 minimal pairs of short phrases, validated by five annotators, whose two versions differ in a moral standard, in another kind of norm (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics or evidence) or in a descriptive quality, and showed them to 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma and Qwen, 1B to 14B, base and instruction-tuned), with and without the word "morally". In every model, the heads that change the moral answer belong to an evaluation circuit the models use for every kind of normative judgment we tested: these heads carry the same share of the effect for moral as for other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00, 97.5% confidence interval [0.92, 1.07], with the word; 0.90, [0.84, 0.96], without it), and the models need them as much for both. The models need these heads also when nothing in the prompt asks for a judgment, and on 400 scenarios of the ETHICS benchmark, where removing them takes away 37 to 39% of the difference between acceptable and unacceptable scenarios, against 1 to 3% for ten random heads. The SAE features we located respond mostly to the word "morally" rather than to what the phrase is about. The models represent the category of a pair (the standard the annotators assigned to it): it can be read from their hidden states, and, in the eight models we tested, removing the direction that carries it weakens the moral verdict by a few percent, and more than the other verdicts in seven of them. We release the pairs, the ratings, the code, the trained SAE dictionaries and the result files.

# Title: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign

> Abstract: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.

# Title: Margin Dynamics for Large Language Model Alignment

> Abstract: Practitioners choose among LLM alignment methods largely by trial and error. # Title: TUSI: A Citation-Grounded Graph-Based Benchmark

> Abstract: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Furthermore, we propose a graph-based retrieval baseline that leverages relational structure within the legal knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines, highlighting the importance of structured legal representations for RAG systems. # Title: Coordination of Heterogeneous Teams with Uncertain Task Requirements

> Abstract: Coordinating a team of heterogeneous agents to complete tasks with unknown requirements is a challenging multi-agent planning problem. # Title: Inventa: Decentralized Self-Improving Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery

> Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can generate research ideas and improve scientific discovery through iterative experimentation. However, increasing the number of agents or iterations does not automatically translate to producing more diverse or feasible ideas. Agents may converge on similar candidates, propagate unsupported claims through shared memory components and repeatedly apply search strategies that no longer yield any improvements. We introduce Inventa, a framework for automated scientific discovery that employs autonomous research units and verified shared knowledge. Each unit creates a lineage of candidate ideas using a mutator agent. A local orchestrator agent periodically adapts the mutator's harness. When progress stalls, the orchestrator agent replaces its model or restarts the idea evolution process. Verifiers evaluate each candidate idea and record verified improvements, useful components and constraint violations in a shared knowledge, the only channel between units. We evaluate Inventa on five benchmarks spanning the research cycle, covering retrieval (ScholarCatalyst), ideation (IdeaBench), proposal writing (IdeaScientist), and scientific law discovery (EurekaBench, SciLaws-Bench). It leads all five, achieving 73.6% on EurekaBench versus 56.2% for CORAL. On IdeaBench, it discovers 26.0 novel ideas per paper, compared with 18.6 for ResearchAgent, with 82% fewer model calls.

# Computer Science > Machine Learning

# Title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler

> Abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.

# Title: PromptPack: Training-Free Augmentation of Diffusion Editors for Intent-Aligned Spatial and Semantic Control

> Abstract: Many image-editing tasks require confining changes to intended spatial regions while exactly preserving user-designated source content. # Computer Science > Machine Learning

# Title: Cancellation-Free Constrained SquareCB for Safe Controller Selection

> Abstract: We study constrained contextual bandits, in which a learner chooses one of $K$ actions in each round to minimize loss while keeping the expected cost of its play below a budget. Existing reductions to online regression weight the cost by a Lagrange multiplier learned from past constraint residuals, so slack in some rounds can offset violations in others. We instead run SquareCB proposed in \citep{foster2020beyond} with a rectified weight on the cost: it is zero when the estimated cost is within the budget, and otherwise just large enough to bring it back to the budget. Under realizability and Slater's condition with margin $\delta$, the algorithm attains regret $O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)}/\delta)$ and cancellation-free violation $\sum_t(V_c^{p_t}-b)^+=O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)})$, where $\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}$ is the error of the regression oracle. The same bounds hold when the budget must be met in every context, potentially adversarially chosen contexts. In controller selection for a safe-control-gym quadrotor and a BOPTEST building, the violation is 6 to 9 times lower than that of primal-dual and virtual-queue baselines, with a lower or comparable regret.

# Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

# Title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights

> Abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

# Title: A Temporal Algebraic Framework for Data Stream Evaluation Under Delayed Labels and Distribution Shifts

> Abstract: In data streams, labels often arrive late or only for some instances, class prevalence drifts, and rare classes vanish from short windows. Standard evaluation then confuses a degraded decision boundary with a change in prevalence, and is biased when labels are delayed or selected by the model. We extend an algebraic framework that obtains pooled (micro) and per-class (macro) measures from one confusion matrix to streams, weighting the counts in time by exponential fading or a sliding window; the update costs O(m^2) per step, whatever the stream length, and each pooled measure stays a weighted combination of the per-class ones. Delayed and selective feedback enter as an observation mask: until its label arrives, an instance is counted with the model's calibrated class probabilities, and the bias of this interim estimate is driven by their calibration error. Audited conventions report no value for a class without verified instances. We separate prior shift from concept drift by monitoring prior-free coordinates (recall and specificity) and attribute a change in a measure to the two sources with a first-order Jacobian decomposition. On synthetic streams and four real datasets, a detector on these coordinates with a memory per class raises no excess false alarms under label shift, unlike the Jacobian alarm and error-rate detectors. The correction for delayed labels recovers recall in some real settings and is only partial for precision, specificity and F1. # Title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding

> Abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.

# Title: Does the Model Use What It Cites? Counterfactual Tests of Grounded Reasoning Chains in Small Video-Language Models

> Abstract: A grounded reasoning chain cites a frame span and a box for every step, so a reader can check where the model looked. Whether the answer depends on the cited region is a different question. We test it by intervention: the regions a model cited in its own chain are blacked out, and the share of correct answers that flip is compared with blacking out boxes of the same size elsewhere on the same frames. The paired difference, the cite gap, needs no annotation. We apply it to 2-3B video-language models trained on exact CLEVRER chains and on pseudo-labelled NExT-QA chains. With the same weights, the cite gap is 0.089 on CLEVRER and 0.003 on NExT-QA. Pooled over models, masking the cited boxes flips 2.2 times as many correct answers as the control on CLEVRER and 1.1 times as many on NExT-QA, also among the answers that depend on the video at all, while the boxes pass a grounding check on both. Masking the cited entity on every frame, instead of the cited box, flips 1.9 times as many answers as its control. The NExT-QA chains were supervised to cite two frames of entities that stay visible on most frames, so this outcome is what the supervision predicts; the point is that the usual check on grounded chains cannot see it. A citation can be verifiable and relevant without the answer depending on it, and a test of grounded reasoning should remove what a chain names, not only where it points.

# Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

# Title: Conserved Verdicts, Drifting Commitments: Identifying Harmful Overthinking

> Abstract: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework says what to measure before building a stopping rule.

# Computer Science > Machine Learning

# Title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor

> Abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.

> Abstract: Predicting the effects of genetic perturbations requires models that generalize beyond observed cell contexts and gene combinations. # Title: Modeling Document and Section Hierarchies in Embedding Space

> Abstract: Embedded topic models integrate word embeddings into the topic generation process, producing coherent topics and robust performance on large vocabularies. However, each document is represented by a single topic distribution, ignoring its internal structure. # Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

# Title: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations

> Abstract: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.
